items.title: [Sports Science 101 #9] You Don't Get Stronger in the Gym — You Get Stronger in Bed
items.body:
> Training is just the stimulus. The actual improvement — stronger muscles, better endurance, sharper skills — is built during recovery, and sleep is where most of that construction happens.

## Today's Concept

Here's a sentence that surprises almost everyone new to sports science: **a workout makes you temporarily worse, not better.**

When you lift weights, run intervals, or play a hard pickup game, you create stress — tiny amounts of muscle damage, depleted energy stores, fatigue in your nervous system. If you measured your performance right after, it would be *below* your normal level.

What happens next is the interesting part. Given enough rest and fuel, your body doesn't just repair itself back to where it was. It rebuilds slightly *above* baseline, as insurance against the next time you face that same stress. Sports scientists call this **supercompensation**. Train again during that elevated window, and your fitness ratchets upward over weeks and months. That's what "getting in shape" actually is.

The cycle looks like this:

```
Stress (training) -> Fatigue (temporary dip) -> Recovery -> Supercompensation (new, higher baseline)
```

Two things can break the cycle:

1. **Too much stress, too little recovery.** If you pile on hard sessions before your body finishes rebuilding, each workout starts from a lower baseline. Performance stalls or declines, sleep and mood suffer, and small injuries start stacking up. In its chronic form, this is called overtraining syndrome.
2. **Skimping on sleep.** Deep sleep (also called slow-wave sleep) is when your body releases most of its growth hormone and does the bulk of physical repair. REM sleep, which comes in longer stretches toward morning, helps consolidate motor skills — the free-throw motion or swim stroke you practiced gets "saved" overnight. Cut sleep short and you cut both processes short. Research on adolescent athletes has linked chronically sleeping under 8 hours per night with noticeably higher injury rates, and lab studies consistently show slower reaction times and reduced endurance after sleep restriction.

The takeaway isn't "train less." It's that **rest is a training input, not the absence of training** — as deliberate a part of the plan as sets, reps, and miles.

## In Everyday Life

Meet Dana, an office worker in Chicago training for their first 10K, the annual race along the lakefront. For six weeks, running four days a week, Dana improves steadily. Then they get ambitious: six runs a week, plus cutting sleep to 6 hours to fit in 5 a.m. workouts before the commute.

Three weeks later, Dana is *slower*. Their easy 3-mile loop feels like a grind, their legs are heavy all day, and a nagging ache has shown up in one knee. Dana's instinct says "I'm losing fitness — I should run more." Sports science says the opposite: Dana has been interrupting the recovery half of the cycle, so every run starts from a deeper hole.

The fix is boring but effective: back down to four runs, protect 7–9 hours of sleep, and keep one or two days fully easy or off. Within two weeks, the same loop feels smooth again — not because Dana trained harder, but because the adaptations finally had time to land.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Training temporarily lowers performance; recovery rebuilds it slightly higher than before — that rebound is called supercompensation.
2. Deep sleep drives physical repair (growth hormone), while REM sleep helps lock in motor skills learned during practice.
3. Persistent fatigue, stalled progress, and recurring minor injuries are signs of too much stress and too little recovery — the answer is usually more rest, not more training.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1. (O/X)** Your muscles actually get stronger during the workout itself.

**Q2.** Supercompensation refers to:
- (a) Eating extra calories after a hard workout
- (b) The body rebuilding to a slightly higher fitness level than before, after stress plus recovery
- (c) Doubling your training volume every week
- (d) Taking supplements to speed up recovery

**Q3.** Which sleep stage is most closely tied to physical repair and growth hormone release?
- (a) REM sleep
- (b) Light sleep
- (c) Deep (slow-wave) sleep
- (d) The few minutes right before waking

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Supercompensation** — The temporary rise in fitness above your previous baseline that follows a training stress plus adequate recovery.
- **Slow-wave (deep) sleep** — The sleep stage dominated by physical restoration, including most of the night's growth hormone release.
- **REM sleep** — The sleep stage linked to memory and motor-skill consolidation; occurs in longer periods toward morning.
- **Overtraining syndrome** — A chronic state of declining performance, fatigue, and mood disturbance caused by long-term imbalance between training stress and recovery.
- **Active recovery** — Very light activity (easy walking, gentle cycling) on rest days that promotes blood flow without adding meaningful training stress.

---

*Answers: Q1 — X. The workout is the stimulus; the strengthening happens afterward, during recovery. Q2 — (b). Supercompensation is the above-baseline rebound after stress and rest. Q3 — (c). Deep, slow-wave sleep is when most physical repair and growth hormone release occur; REM is more associated with skill and memory consolidation.*

items.title: [SCS 2025] What Time Is It in Ancient Rome? The Prize-Winning Book That Rebuilds the Roman Day, Hour by Stretchy Hour
items.body:
> James Ker's *The Ordered Day*, honored with the Society for Classical Studies' 2025 Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit, reconstructs how ancient Romans invented, scheduled, and lived by a day very different from our own — and why their "daily grind" still shapes how we imagine Rome.

## What Was Presented

The Society for Classical Studies (SCS) gives its Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit to outstanding scholarly books in classics — it is widely regarded as the field's most prestigious book prize. One of the 2025 awards went to *The Ordered Day: Quotidian Time and Forms of Life in Ancient Rome* (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2023) by James Ker, a professor of Classical Studies at the University of Pennsylvania.

Classicists have long studied Rome's "big time" — calendars, festivals, eras, and emperors' anniversaries. Ker turns instead to what he calls small time: the single day, from cockcrow to lamplight. His question sounds simple but turns out to be profound: how did Romans come to think of the day as something that could be divided, measured, scheduled, and judged?

The answer was not obvious, because a Roman day was not our day. Romans split daylight into twelve hours and night into twelve more — which meant the length of an "hour" changed with the seasons. In midsummer a daylight hour in Rome stretched to roughly 75 modern minutes; in midwinter it shrank to about 45. Sundials tracked these elastic hours, and water clocks took over at night or under clouds. According to a famous story in Pliny the Elder, Rome's first public sundial was war booty, seized from the Sicilian city of Catania in 263 BCE — and because it was calibrated for the wrong latitude, Romans reportedly read time slightly wrong from it for about a century without much complaint.

Ker traces how, over time, Romans assembled the ingredients of genuine "clock time": partitioning the day into units, scheduling activities with precision, building timekeeping devices, and shifting the authority over time from the sun itself to human instruments and institutions. He then shows how literature acted as a kind of time technology in its own right. Authors such as Cicero, Horace, Martial, Seneca, Pliny the Younger, and Marcus Aurelius described daily routines — the dawn *salutatio* (clients greeting their patron), business in the Forum, afternoon baths, the evening *cena* (dinner) — and in doing so taught readers what a well-ordered, or badly ordered, day looked like. Even the emperor's personal routine, Ker argues, functioned as a timepiece the whole empire could set itself by.

A final section follows the Roman day into later centuries: early Christian monks reworked it into fixed hours of prayer, and modern "daily life in ancient Rome" handbooks still organize everything we know about Romans around the frame of a single day.

## Why It Matters

First, the book flips a familiar assumption. We tend to think schedules arrived with factories, trains, and wristwatches. Ker shows that a sophisticated culture of daily scheduling — appointments at fixed hours, complaints about wasted time, moralizing about early risers and late sleepers — was already thriving two thousand years ago, without a single mechanical clock.

Second, it shows that time is social before it is technical. In Rome, when you woke, when you were greeted, when you bathed, and when you dined signaled who you were: patron or client, farmer or senator, industrious citizen or decadent idler. Daily routine was a language of status and virtue. That insight lands close to home for anyone whose calendar app, commute, and lunch hour quietly define their identity today.

Third, the award itself is a signal. By honoring a book about ordinary, repeated, unglamorous time — rather than wars or dynasties — the SCS highlighted a broader turn in the humanities toward everyday life as serious history.

## An Easy Way to Understand It

Think of the Roman hour as a rubber band. Our modern hour is a rigid steel ruler: 60 minutes, always, everywhere. The Roman hour stretched and shrank with the sun — long and lazy in June, short and tight in December — because there were always exactly twelve of them between sunrise and sunset. Now imagine your phone's calendar built on rubber-band hours: your 9 a.m. meeting drifts with the season, and everyone simply adjusts. Ker's book explains how an entire empire ran — quite smoothly — on that stretchable schedule, and how the routines built on it (greet, work, bathe, dine) became the "operating system" of Roman social life.

## In Three Lines

1. James Ker's *The Ordered Day* (Johns Hopkins, 2023) won the SCS's 2025 Goodwin Award of Merit for showing how ancient Romans made the day a measured, scheduled unit of life.
2. Roman hours stretched with the seasons, yet Romans built a rich culture of timekeeping — sundials, water clocks, and literary "daily routines" that encoded social rank and moral worth.
3. The Roman day outlived Rome: monastic prayer hours and modern daily-life handbooks still use it as a framework, proving that "small time" carries big history.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Goodwin Award of Merit**: The Society for Classical Studies' top annual prize for outstanding scholarly books in classical studies.
- **Quotidian time**: "Everyday" time — the recurring rhythm of a single day, as opposed to calendars, years, and eras.
- **Seasonal hours**: The Roman system dividing daylight and night into twelve hours each, so an hour's length changed throughout the year.
- **Salutatio**: The early-morning ritual in which clients called on their patron at home to pay respects, opening the elite Roman day.
- **Clepsydra**: A water clock that measured time by regulated water flow, used when sundials failed — at night or on cloudy days.
